record.paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
record.context_brief: Formation of WN2 and WN3h helium-ionizing sources
record.original_question: How can stellar-evolution and population-synthesis models reproduce observed WN2 and WN3h Wolf-Rayet stars, especially cases with no detectable companion, while also accounting for their role as strong helium-ionizing sources? A successful answer must explain the formation of early-type WN stars in subsolar-metallicity environments, the absence of plausible dark massive companions for the Small Magellanic Cloud WN3 stars, and the hard ionizing flux that such stars may contribute to low-metallicity galaxies.

evidence.quote: While the WN3 stars in the SMC all contain at least some hydrogen, the even hotter WN2 type can be found in the outer regions of the Milky Way, M33, and the LMC, likely also being connected to subsolar metallicity.
The WN3h stars and the direct WN/WO transition show that WR stars can be strong sources of He II ionizing flux throughout at least a significant part of their He-burning lifetime.

Yet, current evolution and population synthesis models essentially cannot reproduce the observed WN2 and WN3h stars, in particular as most of them do not have a companion. For the SMC WN3 stars, a detailed multi-epoch monitoring actually also ruled out essentially all plausible dark massive companions (Schootemeijer et al. 2024), leaving another open question in massive star research.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Wolf–Rayet (WR) stars are evolved, hot, massive stars that have lost most of their hydrogen-rich envelope and exhibit strong, broad emission lines from dense stellar winds. The nitrogen-sequence WN subtypes are ordered by ionization (and effective temperature), with WN2 being the hottest; the suffix "h" (as in WN3h) indicates the presence of residual hydrogen in the atmosphere. Stars of subtypes WN2 and WN3h have optically thin enough winds that they emit a hard ionizing continuum, including photons capable of doubly ionizing helium (energies ≥ 54.4 eV).

Observationally, all six known WN3h stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC, of metallicity Z ≈ 0.2 Z⊙) contain some hydrogen, while still hotter WN2 stars are found in the outer Milky Way, M33, and the Large Magellanic Cloud, suggesting an association with subsolar metallicity. Detailed multi-epoch radial-velocity monitoring of the SMC WN3 stars rules out, at the 95% confidence level, all binary companions more massive than 5 M⊙ with orbital periods shorter than one year, eliminating essentially all plausible dark massive companions (such as black holes or neutron stars) as drivers of envelope removal.

Within this setup, provide a stellar-evolution and population-synthesis framework that simultaneously:

1. Reproduces the formation of apparently single early-type WN stars (WN2 and WN3h) at subsolar metallicity, given that line-driven mass loss is too weak at such metallicities to strip the hydrogen envelope by the standard "Conti" single-star wind-stripping scenario, and that binary mass transfer or merger products with surviving companions are excluded for the SMC WN3h sample.

2. Predicts the correct relative numbers, hydrogen surface abundances, luminosities, and effective temperatures of WN2 and WN3h stars as a function of metallicity, including the direct WN-to-WO transition.

3. Quantifies the He II–ionizing photon production rate of these stars during their core helium-burning lifetimes and embeds it into a population-synthesis prescription able to account for their cumulative contribution to the hard ionizing radiation field of low-metallicity star-forming galaxies.

Identify the physical mechanism (e.g., rotationally induced chemically homogeneous evolution, envelope inflation and pulsation-driven mass loss, episodic eruptive mass loss, optically thick continuum-driven winds, or another process) that achieves all three requirements consistently.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature (2024–2025) confirms this remains an open problem. Schootemeijer et al. (2024) excluded companions >5 M⊙ with periods <1 year for the SMC WN3h sample, and follow-up work (e.g., Pauli et al. 2025 on metal-poor single WR stars; the SDSS-V LVM study of SMC WN3 stars, 2025) explicitly states that no current standard evolution model predicts the present population of weak-lined WN2/WN3 stars in the Magellanic Clouds, and proposes the interplay of optically thick winds and rotation as a candidate mechanism still under investigation.

status_evidence.title: SDSS-V LVM: Detectability of Wolf-Rayet stars and their He II ionizing flux in low-metallicity environments
status_evidence.snippet: no current standard evolution model predicts the present population of weak-lined WN2 and WN3 stars in the Magellanic Clouds
status_evidence.claim: The formation of single early-type WN stars at low metallicity remains unexplained by standard evolution models.

status_evidence.title: Metal-poor single Wolf-Rayet stars: the interplay of optically thick winds and rotation
status_evidence.snippet: Schootemeijer et al. (2024) rule out the presence of companions more massive than 5 M⊙ and orbital periods shorter than one year for all seven WRs at a 95% confidence level
status_evidence.claim: Binary companions are observationally excluded for SMC WN3h stars, leaving the formation channel open.

status_evidence.title: Wolf-Rayet stars (Shenar review)
status_evidence.snippet: Review discussing open problems in WR formation including hard ionizing flux from WN3h and WN/WO stars at low metallicity.
status_evidence.claim: The role of WN3h stars as He II ionizing sources in low-metallicity galaxies is an active open question.
